study_identification_part.si3_author_journal_year: Sampaio et al., Artificial Intelligence In Medicine, 2025
study_identification_part.si4_title: A generalizable normative deep autoencoder for brain morphological anomaly detection: application to the multi-site StratiBip dataset on bipolar disorder in an external validation framework

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: This study proposes a generalizable multivariate normative modeling framework using deep autoencoders to characterize brain morphology, applied to bipolar disorder. It aims to identify brain deviating patterns at subject and group levels.
study_characteristics_part.sc3_study_design_other: This study utilizes an external validation framework, integrating training with an external test set and accounting for biological and site confounding effects.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Comparison of median MDS between HC and BD using Mann-Whitney U test and Cliff's delta effect size; mass-univariate analysis (two-tailed MWU test with FDR correction); ROC curve analysis to assess discrimination power of MDS and MEV (AUC); pairwise feature RE absolute differences (mean heterogeneity); extreme value statistics (top 1% MEV); computation of frequency of abnormality occurrences; pairwise subject overlap coefficient (OC) and Jaccard similarity (J) of abnormal brain maps.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Brain deviating scores were greater, more heterogeneous, and with increased extreme values in the bipolar disorder group, with volumes from the basal ganglia, hippocampus, and adjacent regions emerging as significantly deviating, supporting heterogeneity and personalization in BD.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: The BD group showed a significantly higher MDS median (0.2264) compared to the HC group (0.1988), with the median MDS difference CI not including zero. Several features (CT, GMV, WMV) showed significantly higher deviations in BD, particularly in the right inferior temporal gyrus (CT), and subcortical/limbic regions (hippocampus, striatum, globus pallidus volumes). RE patterns were more heterogeneous in BD (max mean pairwise difference 1.8 ± 6.8) compared to HC (0.59 ± 1.2). The BD group also exhibited a more pronounced extreme value profile, with 7 CT, 4 GMV, and 4 WMV features having at least double the MEV compared to normative and StratiBip HC groups. MDS-based discrimination between BD and HC yielded an AUC-ROC of 0.6129, slightly improving to 0.6218 when using MEV scores. Individual-level abnormalities were 1.9% in BD subjects (approx. 3 features/subject) versus 1.3% in HC (approx. 2 features/subject). The highest prevalence of abnormal occurrences in BD was for WMV adjacent to the left globus pallidus (11%) and GMV of the right thalamus (7.5%). Within-group similarity for abnormal maps was lower in BD (OC=0.60, J=0.23) than HC (OC=0.72, J=0.32), and BD subjects' abnormal profiles overlapped more with HCs (OC=0.67, J=0.27) than within their own group.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: The methodology did not correct for medication or comorbidities in BD subjects; M-ComBat and linear regression for confounder removal have limitations regarding sample size/imbalances and potential non-linear biological effects; uncertainty of MRI-based feature estimation (e.g., CAT12 segmentation challenges in subcortical regions) was not thoroughly evaluated; the AE model is a black-box model, lacks directionality of REs, and difficulty in evaluating false-positive deviations due to absence of ground truth; incomplete assessment of BD across the entire lifespan (young adults only); unequal distribution of sample size and biological covariates among StratiBip sites.
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: The implemented methodology has several limitations regarding the adjustment of biological covariates. For instance, the data was not corrected for medication on BD, therefore we cannot exclude the possibility that the significant group differences and brain deviations may be driven by medication effects. Similarly, we did not account for comorbidities which might be important to distinguish between disorder-specific effects and others. While the utilization of confounder-free data contributes to the development of more interpretable DL models, ComBat and biological covariates linear regression are subject to limitations concerning confounding source modelling. The former relies on a Bayesian framework for statistical inference of site effects, and the estimates may be affected by sample size and imbalances between sites. Second, linear regression, despite its simplicity and ease of implementation, might not fully capture the biological effects if these encompass non-linearities. To date, there is no gold standard to address confounding effects in neuroimaging studies, and both methods are widely employed in literature. On another note, the uncertainty of estimation of the MRI-based features has not been thoroughly evaluated. CAT12 brain tissue segmentation is based on algorithms that may encounter challenges in segmenting small brain regions with mixed tissues (gray and white matter) and borders... Then, our AE-based network exhibits several limitations that warrant consideration. First, as a black-box model, it is challenging to ascertain precisely what the model is learning. This limitation is only partially mitigated by locally tracking the RE, and by the confounder removal pipeline. Second, the RE lacks information about directionality, making it impossible to determine whether a given deviation results from a feature being too low or too high relative to the encoded normative range. This limitation affects potential clinical application...

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The pipeline includes a generalizable confounder removal step, enhancing translational relevance. The individual-level assessment of brain normative deviations and the integration of multimodal data are innovative aspects for personalized medicine and patient stratification.
